explanations: terra: Abraham asks that this become a secure بَلَدًا and that its people receive fruits; inhabited place is expressly joined to safety and provision.

luna: The section names freeing a captive and feeding an orphan or miskīn as the deeds that cross the steep pass; 2:177 directly joins giving wealth to kin, orphans, needy people, travelers, and freeing people from bondage. | terra: Righteousness includes giving wealth despite love of it to the needy and traveler and freeing people; it turns possessed wealth into the very acts defining the steep ascent in surah 90.

luna: The section's steep-pass sequence feeds a person in need on a day of hunger; 2:184 makes feeding a poor person an alternative obligation for those who cannot fast, another specific way food reaches the miskīn.

luna: The section's poor person and its feeding deed belong to one scene; 2:215 answers what to spend by naming parents, kin, orphans, needy people, and travelers, specifying where property should flow. | terra: The answer about spending directs wealth to parents, kin, orphans, the needy, and the traveler, opening possessions toward people whose support or movement has failed.

luna: The section contrasts a mass of wealth kept at ground level with the deed that raises a person; 2:261 depicts spending for God as seed bearing seven ears with many grains, turning the spent possession into multiplied yield. | terra: Wealth spent in God's way becomes a grain rising into seven ears and multiplied yield; release upward and outward answers wealth compacted into a sterile heap.

luna: The section's man says he spent a mass of wealth, while the needy require compassionate help; 2:262 says spending should not be followed by reminders or injury. In the neighboring charity passage, it distinguishes aid from a self-promoting claim.

luna: The section's ascent depends on turning toward the earthbound poor with mercy; 2:263 says a kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by harm, defining the manner of aid in the charitable sequence that continues into 2:264.

luna: The section connects piled wealth, dust, rain-compacted ground, and giving to the poor. In 2:264, dust on a smooth rock is swept bare by a downpour after showy charity, so an apparent covering and expenditure leave no rooted result. | terra: A showy spender is bare rock thinly covered by تُرَابٌ until a downpour strips it; rain, soil, and false expenditure expose how little the apparent heap holds.

luna: Where 2:264's showy charity leaves dust-covered rock bare, 2:265 compares sincere spending to a garden on high ground (“بِرَبْوَةٍ”) that yields fruit in heavy rain or drizzle. It links giving with elevation and lasting yield. | terra: Sincere spenders are a garden on a height whose downpour doubles its fruit, reversing 2:264's rain-stripped dust and the section's rain-beaten ground.
terra: Believers are told to spend from good earnings and from what God brings out of the earth, directly joining ground, provision, and wealth released toward others.
terra: The devil threatens poverty when people are called to spend, exposing fear of becoming destitute as a force that keeps wealth compacted.
luna: The section's ascent comes through giving to the needy; 2:271 praises giving to the poor, including when concealed, contrasting aid with a public display of spending.

luna: The section's dictionary gloss for miskīn (س ك ن, B001) links the word to lost movement; 2:273 describes needy people who “لَا يَسْتَطِيعُونَ ضَرْبًا فِي الْأَرْضِ”. Their inability to travel makes the earth-bound poverty image concrete. | terra: These poor are restrained in God's way and لَا يَسْتَطِيعُونَ ضَرْبًا فِي الْأَرْضِ; their inability to travel concretizes both the stationary miskīn and the dictionary's non-travelling lubad.

luna: The section links giving toward the needy with elevation; 2:274 describes spending wealth by night and day, privately and publicly, with reward from God. It continues the same charitable subject as 2:271, adding the steadiness of giving across circumstances.
terra: Heaped quantities of gold and silver are among the beautified desires of near life; the verse names both the mass and the attachment that make wealth earthward.
terra: Even مِلْءُ ٱلْأَرْضِ ذَهَبًا cannot ransom the one who dies rejecting faith; wealth literally measured by an earthful ends powerless before death.

luna: The section's road upward requires loosening one's grip on gathered wealth; 3:92 says righteousness is not attained until one spends from what one loves, making the costly turn away from attachment explicit.

luna: The section's steep-pass deeds include freeing a neck from bondage; 3:180 says what misers withhold will be put around their necks. It reverses withheld wealth into constriction, opposite the section's act of release. | terra: What the affluent withhold will be made a collar around them at resurrection; retained bounty becomes the fastening that holds its possessor.

luna: The section sets amassed wealth beside people in need; 4:8 says that when inheritance is being divided and relatives, orphans, and poor people are present, they should be given something from it, directing property toward those with little.

luna: The section sets piled wealth alongside the poor who lack it; 4:37 condemns miserliness and concealing God's bounty, a specific reversal of property held close while others remain in need. | terra: The miserly both withhold God's bounty and instruct others to withhold, allowing accumulated wealth to harden into a social practice.
terra: Sedentary believers, apart from the disabled, are distinguished from those who strive with wealth and lives; property may either anchor its holder or become the means of movement.

luna: The section's dictionary sense for لبد (ل ب د, B003) is one who does not travel or leave; 4:97 challenges people who remain behind by asking whether God's earth was spacious enough for them to migrate. The verse makes staying fixed a question of choice, unlike poverty that restricts movement. | terra: Those claiming helplessness are asked whether God's earth was not spacious enough to migrate; 4:98 then distinguishes people whose immobility is real.

luna: The section's stillness image can describe being unable to move; 4:98 exempts men, women, and children who truly lack means and a way out. It marks the boundary between chosen attachment to the earth and constrained immobility. | terra: Helpless men, women, and children cannot devise a plan or find a way, a broader instance of vulnerability expressed as inability to move.

luna: The section's lexicon calls l-b-d (ل ب د, B003) one who does not travel or leave; 4:100 describes emigrants finding broad room and provision in the earth, a direct movement away from being fixed in one place. | terra: The emigrant who moves through the earth finds many refuges and abundance, giving a mobility-and-provision counter-scene to being fixed by need.
terra: A raven works the earth to teach burial of a corpse; bird, ground, and grave meet the dictionary's crouching bird and turbah of the dead in one scene.
terra: Even everything on earth and its equal cannot ransom a disbeliever from judgment; possessions measured by the whole earth reach an absolute limit.
luna: The section makes feeding the needy part of its moral ascent; 5:89 requires feeding ten poor people as one expiation for a broken oath, giving a concrete instance of wealth converted into food.

luna: The section's imagery includes a camel kneeling and feeding the poor; 5:95 includes feeding poor people as an expiation for a hunting violation during pilgrimage, linking a costly animal-related act to provision for those in need.
terra: The Prophet must not drive away humble worshippers seeking their Lord; nearness to the socially lowly outweighs elite pressure and status.
terra: Night is made سَكَنًا, a beneficial cessation of motion; this natural repose clarifies by contrast the deprivation encoded in miskīn's enforced stillness.

luna: The section opposes piled wealth to need and points toward feeding; 6:141 ties the earth's harvest to giving its due on harvest day and forbids waste, turning produce from private abundance toward a claim beyond the owner.
terra: The command to descend is followed by an earthly place of settlement and temporary enjoyment; life on the ground is expressly a limited stay.
terra: Living, dying, and being brought out all occur in relation to the earth, completing 7:24's settlement with its grave and exit.

luna: The section's lexicon says rain packs the earth; 7:57 uses the word “لِبَلَدٍ مَيِّتٍ” for dead land that rain revives with fruit, a reversal in which rain makes ground productive rather than merely pressed down. | terra: Rain is driven to لِبَلَدٍ مَّيِّتٍ and brings out fruits; balad takes the land/soil sense, while water raises provision from what lay dead.

luna: The section links البلد to ground and settlement; 7:58 uses “الْبَلَدُ الطَّيِّبُ” for good land that yields plants while bad land yields little, showing the ground's condition can make abundance or scarcity visible. | terra: The good balad brings vegetation by God's leave while the bad yields only scantily, tying the character of ground to abundance and scarcity.

luna: This is the setup for the section's cited 7:176: 7:175 introduces the person given God's signs who “فَانْسَلَخَ مِنْهَا”, so the next ayah's failure to rise by them reads as a chosen turning away from what could elevate him. | terra: This ayah identifies the man as one given God's signs who stripped himself from them; it makes 7:176's earthward clinging a response to revelation, as in surah 90's بِـَٔايَٰتِنَا.

luna: The section's vertical axis says ascent comes by turning toward the earthbound; 7:176 says the man could have been raised by the signs but instead “أَخْلَدَ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ”. This names the same reversal from elevation to attachment to earth. | terra: The man could have been raised through the signs, but أَخْلَدَ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ, clung to the earth; this states the section's vertical choice almost exactly.
luna: After the earth-clinging example in 7:176, 7:177 calls the example of those who deny God's signs evil; it completes the link the section draws between descent toward earth and denial of signs.
terra: Fear of poverty is answered by God's promise of enrichment from His bounty, so anticipated want need not harden people into withholding.

luna: The section's “مَالًا لُّبَدًا” makes gathered wealth a central image; 9:34 condemns hoarding gold and silver instead of spending in God's path, an explicit boundary between amassed property and beneficial use. | terra: Hoarded gold and silver are paired with refusal to spend in God's way, defining the moral danger of wealth kept compact instead of released toward need.

luna: The section places rich and poor on the same earth; 9:35 turns hoarded gold and silver into a brand on the hoarders' bodies, reversing wealth from possession into punishment. | terra: The hoard of 9:34 is heated and pressed onto foreheads, sides, and backs; stored wealth becomes a material weight upon the body that amassed it.

luna: The section describes the Qur'anic choice between ascent and remaining pressed down; 9:38 rebukes those summoned to go forth who “اثَّاقَلْتُمْ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ”, making attachment to earth a chosen failure to move. | terra: The summons to go forth meets people who ٱثَّاقَلْتُمْ إِلَى ٱلْأَرْضِ, grow heavy toward the earth, making attachment to the nearer life bodily immobility.
terra: The command to go forth light or heavy and strive with wealth and lives directly reverses 9:38's earthward heaviness and shows wealth put into motion.
terra: The unwilling would travel for nearby gain and an easy journey but find the distance too great, showing material advantage governing whether bodies leave the ground.

luna: The section makes the needy miskīn a recipient of the steep-pass act; 9:60 names the poor and needy among the recipients of alms, specifying a distribution of wealth toward those with little. | terra: Obligatory alms belong to the poor, the needy, and the stranded traveler among others; accumulated property is assigned to both want and interrupted movement.
terra: A promise to give charity if granted bounty sets the proper outward movement of abundance before 9:76 records its reversal.
terra: When bounty arrives, the recipients become miserly and turn away; increase itself produces closure instead of the promised care for others.
terra: Those staying behind rejoice in sitting and dislike striving with wealth and lives; possession and attachment produce the dictionary's person who will not travel.
terra: Men of means request exemption so they can be among the sitters, again making abundance rather than incapacity the cause of immobility.
terra: The weak, ill, and those lacking anything to spend are excused from going forth, distinguishing need-enforced stillness before the weeping would-be travelers of 9:92.
terra: Poor believers want to travel but turn back weeping because no mount can be found; want of property literally fixes them in place.
terra: The blame falls on affluent men who ask to remain with those left behind; beside 9:92, abundance and lack produce the two forms of earthbound stillness developed in the section.
terra: No expenditure small or great and no valley crossed goes unrecorded; the ayah unites the source expression's little-or-much wealth with actual departure and passage.
terra: Every wrongdoing soul would offer all that is on earth as ransom when punishment is seen, making earth-filled possession powerless at the final reckoning.
terra: Night is made for rest and day for sight, placing stillness inside a sustaining rhythm rather than making it the permanent condition of poverty.
terra: God produced humanity from earth and settled or enabled it to flourish there, making attachment to ground a constructive trust rather than moral collapse.
terra: Those who do not answer God would ransom themselves with all the earth's contents and as much again, another exact earth-measure of futile abundance.
terra: Abraham asks that هَٰذَا ٱلْبَلَدَ be secure, echoing surah 90's demonstrative city while 14:37 supplies settlement in its barren ground and the prayer for fruit.
terra: Abraham says أَسْكَنتُ of settling his family in an uncultivated valley, then asks for provision; settlement, barren ground, mobility, and sustenance converge.
terra: The Prophet is told not to fix his eyes on others' worldly enjoyment but to lower his wing to believers; material height is exchanged for deliberate social lowering.
terra: Pack animals carry burdens to a بَلَدٍ reachable only with bodily hardship, joining the city, travel, weight, and the labor required to overcome staying in place.
terra: Water from the sky gives life to earth after its death, reversing the lexicon's rain-compressed soil through a life-giving transformation.

luna: The section places a rich man and a poor person on the same earthly plane; 16:71 asks why people given more provision do not share it with those under their authority, presenting unequal provision as a relationship of withheld goods.

luna: The section's lexicon says a bird can be لبد (ل ب د, B003), crouched on the ground; 16:79 instead points to birds held in the sky, a specific reversal from the grounded bird to one borne aloft. | terra: Birds held in the open sky provide the direct vertical opposite of the dictionary's bird crouched and stuck upon earth.

luna: The section explains لبد (ل ب د, B001) through felt made as fibers pressed into a layer and also names the person who stays put; 16:80 names wool and animal hair made into furnishings and homes as “سَكَنًا”. The verse supplies the material and dwelling side of that image, though it does not describe the felting process. | terra: Homes are made سَكَنًا while hide tents are light on travel and encampment days; the ayah itself distinguishes chosen repose from the inability to depart.
terra: A settled town receives provision abundantly from every direction, then is clothed in hunger after ingratitude; plenty and destitution occupy the same place in succession.
terra: Lowering the wing of humility in mercy toward vulnerable parents gives the section's claim a bodily ethic: moral height appears through deliberate lowering toward another.

luna: The section's upward passage is concrete help for the poor; 17:26 commands giving the miskīn and traveler their due, making the earthbound person a rightful recipient of wealth. | terra: Giving the needy and traveler their due directs property toward both poverty and movement, the two pressures gathered in the stationary miskīn image.

luna: The section pairs a claim of having spent heaps with care for the poor; 17:27 calls reckless spenders brothers of devils, marking a boundary between boastful depletion and directed aid such as 17:26 commands.

luna: The section's wealth-rich man says he spent a great mass; 17:29 warns against a closed hand and against spending without limit, setting a boundary around the handling of wealth beside the poor's due. | terra: The hand must be neither chained to the neck nor extended without limit; provision is released without turning the giver into someone stripped and grounded by want.
terra: The arrogant walker can neither split the earth nor reach the mountains in height; human pretension is bounded between ground and elevation.
terra: If humans possessed the treasuries of divine mercy, they would withhold them from fear of spending, exposing the impulse that compresses abundance into a guarded mass.
terra: The Children of Israel are told to dwell in the land, then are gathered at the final promise; settled residence eventually yields to divinely compelled movement.
terra: The addressee must remain with humble worshippers and not let his eyes pass beyond them toward worldly adornment, a social form of bending toward the lowly rather than wealth.

luna: The section's wealthy man boasts of having spent “مَالًا لُّبَدًا”; 18:34 gives the garden owner’s comparison, “أَنَا أَكْثَرُ مِنكَ مَالًا”, making wealth a basis for status over another person. | terra: The garden-owner boasts that he is greater in wealth and stronger in followers, a narrative counterpart to the boast over piled wealth in 90:6.

luna: The section places abundant wealth beside the poor person's earth-bound state; 18:35 has the garden owner enter his property convinced it will never perish, exposing the false permanence that the section's grave and soil senses unsettle.
terra: A rich garden-owner who boasts of wealth is reminded that his Creator made him مِن تُرَابٍ; the rebuke puts the affluent man on the same dust as the destitute.

luna: The section's dictionary also gives the reversal “no little or much” for לبد (ل ب د, B007); 18:42 depicts the garden owner's fruit and wealth destroyed, leaving him regretful over what he had spent. The former abundance collapses toward nothing. | terra: The boaster's produce is destroyed and he turns his hands over what he spent while the garden lies collapsed, bringing vaunted property physically down.

luna: The section's piled wealth is set against the earth-bound poor; 18:45 pictures worldly life as rain-fed growth that dries and is scattered by wind, making abundant material life visibly temporary.

luna: The section distinguishes piled wealth from the deeds that raise a person; 18:46 calls wealth and children adornment of worldly life but says enduring good deeds are better in reward and hope. | terra: Wealth and children are the adornment of near life, while enduring good deeds are better in reward and hope; possession is denied lasting vertical worth.

luna: The section links miskīn (س ك ن, B001) with stillness; 18:79 calls the boat owners “لِمَسَاكِينَ يَعْمَلُونَ فِي الْبَحْرِ”, poor people actively working at sea. Their movement marks a useful boundary: the Qur'anic poverty term does not itself mean motionless.

luna: The section's lexicon says turbah for the dead is a grave (ت ر ب, B001) and traces البلد to grave or soil (ب ل د, B001); 20:55 says humanity is created from earth, returned to it, and brought out from it, placing both wealth and poverty under the same mortal ground. | terra: Human beings are created from earth, returned into it, and brought out again; soil is origin, grave, and the point from which immobility will be reversed.
terra: Human origin in تُرَابٍ is joined to lifeless earth that trembles and swells after water; the same ground that receives bodies visibly rises.
terra: Following 22:5's dust-origin and rain-raised ground, this ayah states that God will raise those in graves; burial's stillness is explicitly temporary.

luna: The section names feeding the hungry and the poor as the steep-pass work; 22:28 tells pilgrims to eat from sacrificial livestock and feed the needy who ask, an earlier formulation in the same sacrificial passage as 22:36. | terra: Pilgrims eat from sacrificial animals and feed the afflicted poor, so an animal brought down becomes provision for someone brought low by need.

luna: The section's BLD entry describes a camel putting its chest on the ground when it kneels; 22:36 pictures sacrificial camels whose sides fall, then commands people to eat and feed the needy. The animal's lowering becomes provision for others. | terra: The sacrificial animals stand, then their sides fall to earth and their flesh feeds the content and the beggar; bodily descent becomes provision for someone in need.
terra: Water descends and the earth becomes green; the surface responds to rain with visible life rather than remaining a compacted layer.
terra: Measured rain is made to settle in the earth, فَأَسْكَنَّاهُ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ; the س ك ن root here gives life by coming to rest rather than naming deprivation's arrested motion.

luna: The section's moral turn is to give toward vulnerable people; 24:22 urges pardon and continued support for relatives, poor people, and migrants even after personal hurt, giving a concrete test of generosity. | terra: People of abundance are forbidden to stop giving to kin, the needy, and emigrants; wealth and social elevation must bend toward those exposed by need and displacement.
terra: Those who are poor are promised enrichment from God's bounty within a command of communal care, presenting poverty and sufficiency as transformable conditions.

luna: The section names freeing a captive as part of the passage upward; 24:33 tells owners to help enslaved people seeking emancipation from the property God has given them, making wealth a means of release.
terra: Birds glorify with wings outspread, another explicit airborne posture opposite the dictionary's bird crouched against earth.
terra: Rain revives بَلْدَةً مَّيْتًا and waters animals and many people; dead ground becomes the means of relieving bodily need.

luna: The section juxtaposes abundant wealth with the needy person's lack; 25:67 describes good spending as neither wasteful nor miserly, a specific boundary that corrects both unbounded depletion and withholding.
terra: The day when neither wealth nor children benefit sets a direct boundary on what the amassed heap can carry beyond earthly life.
terra: Lowering one's wing to believing followers repeats the bodily ethic of descending toward people under one's care.
terra: Night in which people rest is a divine sign, another positive use of the س ك ن root against involuntary social immobility.
terra: The speaker is commanded to worship the Lord of this بَلْدَة, who made it sacred; the city is a divinely bounded settled place rather than mere soil.
terra: Night is given so people may rest, لِتَسْكُنُوا, and day so they may seek bounty; wholesome stillness alternates with provision-seeking movement.

luna: The section's wealth-mass image is sharpened by Qarun: 28:76 depicts the immense weight of his treasure keys, making abundance itself a burden before the earth swallows him in 28:81. | terra: Qarun's treasure keys burden a strong company; abundance is represented as compact, bodily weight before the earth swallows it in 28:81.

luna: The section says ascent comes by using wealth to turn toward the lowly; 28:77 tells Qarun to seek the Hereafter with what God gave him and to do good, giving an explicit ethical direction to abundance. | terra: Qarun is told to seek the final abode through what God gave him and to do good; wealth could raise its holder only by being redirected from self-attachment.

luna: The section puts wealth and the soil-bound poor on one horizontal plane; 28:81 makes Qarun's great wealth end when he and his house are swallowed by the earth, a stark reversal of riches as security. | terra: The owner of immense treasure is swallowed together with his house by the earth, making amassed wealth and downward attachment one literal scene.

luna: After Qarun and his house are swallowed by earth in 28:81, 28:82 says onlookers recognize that God expands and restricts provision. It reverses their envy of his wealth and echoes the section's shared plane of plenty and want. | terra: Those who wished for Qarun's station recognize that provision is expanded or restricted and that they too could have been swallowed, undoing the equation of abundance with height.
terra: Rain sent from the sky revives earth after death; repeated Qur'anic formulation makes water an agent of release and life rather than mere flattening.
terra: A secure sanctuary is set amid people being snatched away around it, clarifying the Meccan city's character as stable refuge within dangerous movement.
terra: Created مِن تُرَابٍ, humans then تَنتَشِرُونَ, spread abroad; dust-origin issues in dispersal and movement rather than adhesion to the ground.
terra: Rainwater revives earth after its death, embedding the upward recovery of ground within the signs of lightning, fear, and hope.
terra: At one call people emerge from the earth; the final divine summons reverses the stillness of burial immediately and bodily.

luna: The section presents helping the needy as the means of ascent; 30:38 commands giving relatives, the poor, and travelers their due, placing the share of the earthbound within the giver's property. | terra: Giving the needy and traveler their due places property at the service of both destitution and mobility.
terra: The effects of divine mercy are visible in earth revived after death, and that reviver will raise the dead; soil's recovery becomes the model for bodies leaving it.
terra: Saba's dwelling is a sign with two gardens and the words بَلْدَةٌ طَيِّبَةٌ; balad here is an inhabited, provision-bearing ground rather than grave-soil.
terra: Saba's turn from gratitude brings a flood and replacement of its abundant gardens with meager growth, reversing 34:15's good, provision-bearing balad.
terra: Clouds are driven to a dead بَلَدٍ and the earth is revived; rain's effect is life and lifting rather than the lexicon's compression of soil.
terra: All people are ٱلْفُقَرَاءُ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ while God alone is rich, collapsing the earthly distinction between the possessor of the heap and the destitute beside him.
terra: Those in graves cannot be made to hear; the grave is pictured through the stillness and unresponsiveness that the section associates with lost movement.

luna: The section turns wealth from a boast into help for the earthbound poor; in 36:47, disbelievers refuse to feed those in need by asking whether they should feed people God could feed, a pointed reversal of wealth as a means of mercy.
terra: At the trumpet people rush from graves to their Lord; movement erupts from the place that had held the dead motionless.
terra: Wrongdoers would offer all that is on earth and its like as ransom; the imagined earth-sized fortune cannot lift its possessor from judgment.
terra: Night is made for rest and day for sight through divine bounty, connecting repose to provision while distinguishing it from need that arrests movement.
terra: Earth seen خَاشِعَةً stirs and swells when water descends, a precise upward reversal of soil flattened and matted by rain.
terra: Measured water revives a dead بَلْدَةً, followed by the comparison to being brought out; the soil sense of balad opens onto resurrection.

luna: The section distinguishes earthly wealth from the ascent made through mercy and help; 43:32 says God apportions provision and raises some people above others in worldly ranks, yet God's mercy is better than what they accumulate.
terra: Provision sent from the sky revives earth after death, joining rain, ground, and sustenance in the opposite movement from pressed barrenness.

luna: The section treats riches and poverty as a shared earthly condition and makes turning wealth outward a source of ascent; 47:38 says people called to spend who withhold only withhold from themselves, since God is rich and they are needy. | terra: People are called to spend but withhold, although وَٱللَّهُ ٱلْغَنِىُّ وَأَنتُمُ ٱلْفُقَرَاءُ; this overturns the rich person's imagined height and locates need universally.
terra: Those who remained behind say أَمْوَٰلُنَا وَأَهْلُونَا شَغَلَتْنَا; wealth itself is offered as what kept its owners from setting out.
terra: Rain is provision for servants and revives a dead بَلْدَةً; emergence from death is compared to produce rising from watered ground.
terra: The earth splits from people as they emerge hurriedly; ground releases the buried into swift movement, reversing both grave enclosure and arrested motion.

luna: The section pairs material abundance with a person stuck in dust; 51:19 says the believers' wealth contains a known right for “السَّائِلِ وَالْمَحْرُومِ”, giving the deprived a claim within the rich person's property. | terra: In their wealth is a right for the asker and the deprived; this directly joins held property to the person scarcity has brought low.
terra: People emerge from graves like scattered locusts, replacing the grave's stillness with dispersal and mass movement.
terra: God's revival of earth after death supplies a repeated boundary to the grave and motionless-soil senses developed in the section.

luna: The section's wealth and soil image concerns what is pressed down and what can rise; 57:20 joins boasting and competition in wealth to vegetation that flourishes after rain, yellows, and becomes debris, setting passing abundance against what endures. | terra: Worldly rivalry in wealth is compared to rain-grown vegetation that dries and becomes debris, making material accumulation part of an earthly cycle that will not remain.
terra: Those who are miserly and command miserliness are answered by God's self-sufficiency, setting the closed human heap against the only true richness.

luna: The section sets the wealthy and needy side by side on the same plane; 59:7 explains distribution of communal wealth so it will not remain “دُولَةً بَيْنَ الْأَغْنِيَاءِ”, supplying a concrete boundary against wealth piling among the rich. | terra: Distribution to orphans, the needy, and travelers is ordered so wealth does not merely circulate among the rich; the rule directly prevents wealth from matting into one social layer.

luna: The section's settled-place and wealth imagery meets people made poor by displacement; 59:8 describes needy emigrants driven from their homes and property who seek God's bounty. It supplies the migrants' own loss that 59:9's generosity answers. | terra: Poor emigrants are expelled from homes and possessions yet move in search of God's bounty, a direct counter-scene to poverty that prevents travel.

luna: The section contrasts a person stuck to earth through plenty with one stuck through want; 59:9 praises people who give others preference even while themselves in need, reversing the expected direction of abundance. | terra: People already settled in the abode prefer displaced newcomers over themselves despite their own privation, joining settlement, scarcity, and the outward release of goods.
terra: After prayer people are told to disperse through the earth and seek God's bounty, the active opposite of both the non-travelling lubad and poverty-enforced stillness.
terra: The hypocrites propose withholding support until the Prophet's companions disperse; wealth is deliberately used to uproot vulnerable people from their place.
terra: Wealth and children must not distract from God's remembrance; possession becomes loss when its accumulated claims hold the owner in the nearer life.

luna: The section sets claimed wealth beside the poor person's need and makes giving a route upward; 63:10 urges spending from God's provision before death arrives, when the regretful person wishes for more time to give charity. | terra: People must spend from provision before death and the futile request for delay; the stored heap must be opened before its owner reaches the grave.

luna: The section opposes piled wealth to giving that carries a person upward; 64:16 urges spending from God's provision and says those protected from their own greed are successful, naming the inward obstacle to releasing wealth.
terra: أَسْكِنُوهُنَّ commands housing vulnerable women where the addressees dwell and according to their means; settled space and material capacity become care rather than exclusion.
terra: Earth is made tractable: people are told to walk its slopes and eat God's provision; ground becomes a traversable source of sustenance rather than a surface that pins one down.

luna: The section's lexicon says a bird can be l-b-d (ل ب د, B003), crouched on the earth; 67:19 instead shows birds above with wings spread and folded, a specific reversal from the section's grounded bird to flight. | terra: Birds above spread and fold their wings while the Merciful holds them; elevation and divine holding reverse the earth-clinging bird sense of lubad.

luna: The section sets the low, earth-pressed words against the surah's raised path; 67:22 contrasts one who walks “مُكِبًّا عَلَىٰ وَجْهِهِ” with one walking upright on a straight path, giving bodily form to the same low/upright divide. | terra: Face-down movement is set against upright walking on a straight path, turning the section's horizontal body and rising road into an explicit test of guidance.

luna: The section's image culminates in feeding the miskīn; the garden owners in 68:24 plan “أَنْ لَا يَدْخُلَنَّهَا الْيَوْمَ ... مِسْكِينٌ”, turning abundant produce into a boundary against the poor. | terra: The garden owners command that no miskīn enter that day; accumulated produce is guarded by excluding the very earthbound poor person the section commands one to approach.

luna: The section pairs one stuck to earth through abundance with one through want; after the garden owners exclude the poor, 68:27 has them recognize “بَلْ نَحْنُ مَحْرُومُونَ”, reversing their former position into deprivation. | terra: After barring the miskīn in 68:24, the owners say بَلْ نَحْنُ مَحْرُومُونَ; those with abundance become the deprived, reversing the two positions.
terra: At judgment the speaker admits that his wealth did not avail him; property that seemed protective has no power at the final descent.

luna: The section makes care of the miskīn part of the difficult ascent; 69:34 describes the condemned person as one who did not urge feeding “الْمِسْكِينِ”, a direct counterpart to the section's ethical turn. | terra: Failure to urge feeding the miskīn is named among the causes of punishment, making neglect of the lowly a decisive spiritual failure.
terra: جَمَعَ فَأَوْعَىٰ presents the person who collects and seals wealth away, a concise parallel to possessions compacted into an unmoving heap.
terra: When good touches the anxious human he becomes withholding; material ease paradoxically arrests outward movement of provision.

luna: The section presents abundance and poverty together and makes aid the ascent; 70:24 says the faithful have a known share in their wealth, which 70:25 identifies for the asker and deprived. | terra: The prayerful have a known right within their wealth; the heap is opened by recognizing that part of it already belongs beyond its possessor.

luna: The section's toprağa yapışmış miskīn is one of the people toward whom the steep pass bends; 70:25 names the share in the preceding ayah as belonging to “السَّائِلِ وَالْمَحْرُومِ”. | terra: The fixed share of 70:24 belongs to the asker and the deprived, placing the needy person structurally inside, rather than outside, accumulated property.
terra: People rush from graves as though racing toward a marker; the formerly earth-held body becomes urgently mobile.
terra: God causes humanity to grow from the earth like a growth; 71:18 then returns them into the same ground and brings them forth.
terra: Return into earth is followed by a decisive bringing forth, so grave-soil is a temporary enclosure rather than permanent sticking.

luna: The section's lexicon identifies لبد (ل ب د, B001–B002) as things piled and pressed together; 72:19 uses “لِبَدًا” for the crowd almost piling onto God's servant as he rises to call on Him. It is the Qur'an's direct occurrence of the section's crowded heap-word. | terra: The only other Qur'anic لِبَدًا pictures people nearly becoming a compact mass upon God's servant, preserving the source word's piled, inseparable layers in a crowd.
terra: Some travel through the earth seeking God's bounty; movement is the means to provision here, clarifying what the immobilized poor of 2:273 cannot do.

luna: The section's deeds include feeding the poor in a day of hunger; 74:44 gives the condemned speakers' own explanation: “وَلَمْ نَكُ نُطْعِمُ الْمِسْكِينَ”. | terra: The condemned confess that they did not feed the miskīn; their own speech identifies the missed act that the steep ascent requires.

luna: The section's steep-pass sequence frees a captive and feeds the needy; 76:8 depicts people giving food “مِسْكِينًا وَيَتِيمًا وَأَسِيرًا”, bringing the miskīn, orphan, and captive together as recipients. | terra: They feed the miskīn, orphan, and captive despite loving the food, enacting the section's claim that ascent requires turning beloved provision toward the lowly.
terra: The earth is made كِفَاتًا, a containing place; 77:26 specifies that its gathered contents are both the living and the dead.
terra: أَحْيَاءً وَأَمْوَاتًا makes one earth hold inhabited life and buried death, joining the settlement and cemetery senses developed for balad.

luna: The section says the poor man's soil is also the rich man's measure of wealth and recalls the wish to become dust; 78:40 gives the denier's “يَا لَيْتَنِي كُنْتُ تُرَابًا” after seeing what his hands sent ahead, reversing poverty's dust into a wished-for refuge. | terra: At judgment the denier wishes, يَٰلَيْتَنِى كُنتُ تُرَابًا; the earth beneath the destitute becomes the wished-for refuge of one whose deeds and possessions cannot save him.
terra: The one who considers himself self-sufficient receives attention, while the vulnerable seeker is neglected in the surrounding scene; the stance reverses the section's demanded inclination.
terra: Being distracted from the earnest blind visitor completes the scene begun in 80:1-2 and 80:5, showing what it means to turn away from someone socially brought low.

luna: The section's root notes equate the dead person's turbah with the grave (ت ر ب, B001); 80:21 says God causes a person to die and be buried (“فَأَقْبَرَهُ”), directly naming what the soil-bound word leads to.
luna: After 80:21's burial, 80:22 says God will raise the person when He wills; this neighboring ayah completes the section's contrast between being laid in earth and being elevated.
terra: Water is poured abundantly before 80:26's splitting of earth; rain initiates opening rather than compression.
terra: ثُمَّ شَقَقْنَا ٱلْأَرْضَ شَقًّا makes the watered ground split apart so food can emerge, the opposite physical movement from felting soil into one layer.
terra: When graves are overturned and their contents thrown out, burial ground can no longer keep bodies pressed within it.

luna: The section's BLD dictionary entry describes a camel kneeling with its chest on the ground; 88:17 opens a sequence by asking people to look at camels and how they were created, recalling the animal in the section's grounded image.

luna: The section contrasts raised heights with words pressed to earth; 88:18 asks how the sky was raised, part of the same 88:17–20 sequence that moves from camel to heaven, mountains, and spread earth.

luna: The section's image sets elevation against a low plane; 88:19 asks how mountains were erected within the sequence from camel to raised sky and spread earth, giving the high side of that contrast.

luna: The section puts its images on the horizontal ground beneath the surah's elevations; 88:20 asks how the earth was spread, completing the neighboring camel/sky/mountain survey with the low plane.

luna: The section places abundant wealth and the needy on the same ground; 89:15 shows a person mistaking expanded provision for honor, exposing wealth as a measure that can mislead rather than lift him.

luna: Where the section's poor person is pressed down by lack, 89:16 shows a person mistaking restricted provision for humiliation. The next verses correct both readings by turning to treatment of the orphan and poor.
luna: The section says ascent is made by bending toward those pressed down; 89:17 rebukes people who “لَا تُكْرِمُونَ الْيَتِيمَ”, naming the failure to honor a vulnerable person.

luna: The section's steep-pass deeds include feeding the poor; 89:18 says people do not urge one another to feed “الْمِسْكِينِ”, the direct ethical opposite of bending toward the earthbound needy. | terra: Failure to urge feeding the miskīn immediately precedes devouring inheritance and loving amassed wealth, supplying the neglected person on the other side of 89:20's heap.

luna: The section sets charity beside a man's claim about consuming heaps of wealth; 89:19 condemns consuming inheritance greedily (“أَكْلًا لَمًّا”), showing accumulated property turned inward instead of toward the needy. | terra: Inheritance is devoured with all-consuming greed between neglect of the poor and love of massed wealth, showing how the heap is produced by taking rather than bending down to give.

luna: The section's lexicon explains لبد (ل ب د, B002) with the dictionary form جمًّا, abundant; 89:20 uses “حُبًّا جَمًّا” for overwhelming love of wealth, directly clarifying the section's “wealth piled in abundance” image. | terra: حُبًّا جَمًّا describes massed, consuming love of wealth; the source itself identifies جَمًّا as the Qur'anic gloss of the piled لُبَدًا.

luna: The section says the steep pass opens through deeds for the lowly; 92:5 begins the contrast with one who gives and is God-fearing, tying expenditure to a moral route. | terra: The one who gives and is mindful begins the opposite course from 92:8's miser; giving is the first movement toward the ease promised in 92:7.
luna: In the same sequence as the giver in 92:5, 92:6 says he affirms the best; this supplies the belief behind the section's contrast between mere wealth spent and giving that leads upward.

luna: The section presents the steep pass as the hard route toward elevation; 92:7 says the giving person will be eased toward ease, an explicit reversal of the burdened earthward posture. | terra: Ease is facilitated for the giver described in 92:5-6, paralleling ascent through releasing wealth toward another.

luna: The section's rich figure is stuck in an abundance that does not raise him; 92:8 describes the opposite of the giver, one who is stingy and sees himself as self-sufficient. | terra: The miser who considers himself self-sufficient, ٱسْتَغْنَىٰ, embodies the dictionary's opposite pole of dust: imagined richness that leaves its owner unwilling to give.
luna: In 92:8–10, the self-sufficient miser's stance is paired with denial of the good; 92:9 names that denial, clarifying the inner turn opposite to the section's ascent by compassion.

luna: The section opposes ascent to being fixed toward the earth; 92:10 says the miser is eased toward hardship, an explicit path-reversal from 92:7's ease for the giver. | terra: Difficulty is facilitated for the miser who deems himself self-sufficient, preparing the fall in 92:11.

luna: The section measures the rich man's mass of wealth against the poor person's soil; 92:11 says his wealth will not avail him when he falls, removing wealth's claim to rescue him. | terra: وَمَا يُغْنِى عَنْهُ مَالُهُ إِذَا تَرَدَّىٰ asks what wealth can do when its owner falls headlong; the heap cannot arrest the downward movement it encouraged.

luna: The section pairs wealth pressed to earth with a poor person pressed into soil; 93:8 recalls that God found the Prophet in need and made him self-sufficient, connecting provision to the following commands about vulnerable people. | terra: God found the addressee عَائِلًا and made him self-sufficient, showing need and sufficiency as reversible conditions rather than fixed human heights.
luna: The section says elevation requires turning toward the lowly; 93:9 commands, “فَأَمَّا الْيَتِيمَ فَلَا تَقْهَرْ”, giving a concrete response to vulnerability.
luna: The section's poor person is a figure to whom one must bend; 93:10 says not to repel the asker (“السَّائِلَ”), making the response to need explicit.
terra: The oath وَهَٰذَا ٱلْبَلَدِ ٱلْأَمِينِ repeats the deictic city of 90:1 and marks that settled ground by security.
terra: Human transgression begins when a person sees himself as self-sufficient; imagined richness supplies the stance behind boastful possession and refusal to give.
terra: Prostrate and draw near makes bodily descent the means of nearness, a compact spiritual parallel to rising by bending toward one already low.
terra: The earth casts out its burdens, turning what lay pressed and hidden within burial ground outward.
terra: Intense love of wealth supplies the attachment whose earthly endpoint appears immediately in the opened graves of 100:9.
terra: When what lies in the graves is scattered out, the intense wealth-love of 100:8 reaches the soil and burial horizon developed in the section.

luna: The section's piled مال and its grave/soil senses meet in 102:1–2: “التَّكَاثُرُ” is competition in increase, and this ayah makes that accumulation the distraction that precedes the grave. | terra: Rivalry in accumulation distracts people; read with 102:2, the activity that builds the heap runs only until its owners reach the graves.

luna: The section traces البلد and turbah to burial ground; 102:2 says people continue competing “حَتَّىٰ زُرْتُمُ الْمَقَابِرَ”. The grave ends the earthly contest over abundance. | terra: حَتَّىٰ زُرْتُمُ الْمَقَابِرَ completes 102:1 by placing accumulators in the cemetery, the terminal soil sense that the section finds inside balad and turbah.

luna: The section's “مَالًا لُّبَدًا” is wealth massed together; 104:2 depicts a person who gathers wealth and counts it (“جَمَعَ مَالًا وَعَدَّدَهُ”), a close image of amassed property. | terra: The person who جَمَعَ مَالًا وَعَدَّدَهُ turns wealth into a counted mass, a direct behavioral form of مَالًا لُبَدًا.

luna: The section sets material abundance beside the dust-bound poor; 104:3 exposes the gathered man's false security, “يَحْسَبُ أَنَّ مَالَهُ أَخْلَدَهُ”, while the section's earthy and grave senses place wealth under mortality. | terra: The collector imagines his wealth makes him endure; 104:4 immediately answers the fantasy with being cast into the Crusher.
terra: لَيُنبَذَنَّ فِى ٱلْحُطَمَةِ answers the counted heap by throwing its owner downward, turning presumed permanence into violent abasement.
terra: The winter and summer journeys define movement away from and back to the settled sacred place; 106:4 states that these journeys culminate in food and security.
terra: Worship of the Lord of this House supplies the fixed sacred center between the journeys of 106:2 and the food and security of 106:4.
terra: The Lord of the House feeds Quraysh against hunger and secures them against fear, placing provision within the same Meccan ground called البلد in surah 90.
luna: The section locates the steep pass in caring for the vulnerable; 107:2 describes the denier as one who thrusts the orphan away, a direct reversal of that care.

luna: The section names feeding the miskīn as a way upward; 107:3 condemns failing even to urge “طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ”, the precise opposite of that act. | terra: The one who does not urge feeding the miskīn is condemned, the direct negative of stooping toward the ground-bound poor through food.
terra: Withholding even ordinary aid completes the passage that refuses food to the miskīn, showing the small, everyday closure behind neglect of the poor.
terra: Abu Lahab's wealth and gains do not avail him, another concise boundary on what a possessed heap can secure.
